title: Multiplying by Z to the alpha preserves back-and-forth relations with a doubled shift
source_title: Scott sentence complexities of linear orderings

standard_prerequisites.name: Multiplication of linear orders by Z to the alpha
standard_prerequisites.statement: Z^alpha times L is the lexicographic product of the order Z^alpha with L, whose elements are pairs (delta, l).
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the operation the lemma relates to the back-and-forth relations.

standard_prerequisites.name: Back-and-forth relations and their intervals
standard_prerequisites.statement: The rank beta relation between two orders is decided by the rank beta minus one relations between the intervals determined by the chosen tuples.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is how the successor step is verified.

core_obligations: Prove the statement by induction on beta, with the base case coming from the observation preceding the lemma and the limit case from the definition of the relations together with the fact that multiplying both sides of a comparison by a fixed order preserves it (source lines 1281-1284).
For the successor step write beta as gamma plus one and read Z^alpha times K as a product ordering whose elements are pairs (delta, b) (source lines 1286-1289).
Answer a tuple played by the opponent with the winning strategy of the comparison at rank gamma plus one, applied coordinatewise to the second components (source lines 1289-1292).

Reduce the required interval comparison to the isomorphism of each interval with zeta_alpha plus Z^alpha times the interval of the original order plus zeta_alpha star, and close it with the induction hypothesis (source lines 1292-1300).

proof_roadmap.step: Base and limit cases of the induction on beta.
Rewrite the product and set up the play of the game.
Answer coordinatewise with the winning strategy for the original comparison.
Compute the two intervals and apply the induction hypothesis.

difficulty_reason: Counted unit is the author labelled lemma at source0.tex lines 1275-1278: for any two countable linear orders, a rank beta comparison between them yields a comparison of rank twice alpha plus beta between their products with Z^alpha. The statement is a rank arithmetic assertion with no witness, and the proof (source lines 1280-1301) has to run an induction on beta in which the successor step is the real work: the product is rewritten as an ordering of pairs, the opponent plays a tuple of pairs, the answer is produced coordinatewise by the winning strategy of the original comparison, and the interval that remains to be compared is identified with a concatenation of two zeta blocks around the product of the corresponding interval, after which the induction hypothesis applies. Neither the coordinatewise strategy nor the interval computation is visible in the statement, and the doubled shift in the rank comes out of the second factor.
